title: Statistics & Data Analysis
relevance: Analyst and quant rounds probe statistical intuition—on-the-fly estimates, why a metric misleads, and Bayes base-rate problems—more than memorizing distribution PDFs.

phases.goal: Establish core descriptive measures, variance/SD identities, linear-transform rules, correlation, the empirical rule, Bayes, and binomial moments.

must_hit.point: Mean is the average and is sensitive to outliers; median is the middle value and is robust to outliers (skewed data); mode is the most frequent value.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts mean vs median under skew and states mode as most frequent.

must_hit.point: Variance is σ² = E[X²] − (E[X])² and standard deviation is σ = √Variance.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the E[X²]−(E[X])² identity and that SD is the square root of variance.

must_hit.point: For Y = aX + b: E[Y] = aE[X] + b, Var(Y) = a² Var(X), and SD becomes |a|σ_X; adding a constant shifts the mean but does not change variance.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates affine effect on mean from scale-only effect on variance/SD.

must_hit.point: Cov(X,Y) = E[XY] − E[X]E[Y]; correlation ρ = Cov(X,Y)/(σ_X σ_Y) with −1 ≤ ρ ≤ 1 measures linear relationship strength.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives the covariance formula, the ρ definition, the [−1,1] range, and linear-strength meaning.

must_hit.point: The 68-95-99.7 rule: ≈68% of normal data within μ ± 1σ, 95% within μ ± 2σ, and 99.7% within μ ± 3σ.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Recalls the three percentages tied to 1σ, 2σ, and 3σ bands.

must_hit.point: Binomial with n trials and success probability p has mean = np and variance = np(1−p).
must_hit.evidence_hint: States both np and np(1−p) without conflating them.

probes: What happens to mean and variance under Y = aX + b, and how does the 68-95-99.7 rule read for a normal?
How are covariance and correlation defined, and what do binomial mean and variance equal?

hints.1: Start with mean/median/mode under outliers, then variance from moments.
hints.2: Write E[Y] and Var(Y) for an affine transform; then ρ = Cov/(σ_X σ_Y) and the empirical-rule percentages.
hints.3: Y = aX + b → mean aE[X]+b, Var a²Var(X), SD |a|σ_X; Var = E[X²]−(E[X])²; 68%/95%/99.7% at 1σ/2σ/3σ; binomial mean np, variance np(1−p).

phases.goal: Show they can recompute means under updates/weights, apply affine SD rules, diagnose skew, recover SD from moments, combine constant groups, and evaluate z-scores, binomial, and Poisson probabilities.

must_hit.point: New mean after adding a point equals (old sum + new value) / (n+1); e.g. 10 numbers mean 40 plus 62 → sum 462 over 11 → mean 42.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Rebuilds sum as n×mean, adds the new value, divides by n+1.

must_hit.point: Combined mean is a weighted average of group means (or baseline-plus-excess deviations); e.g. 20 men at 60000 and 30 women at 50000 → overall 54000.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses total salary / 50 or spreads the men's 10000 excess across 50 employees to get +4000.

must_hit.point: After Y = 1.2X + 5 on scores with mean 60 and SD 8, new mean is 77 and new SD is 9.6 (the +5 does not change spread).
If mean is significantly greater than median (e.g. median 15, mean 45 on a skewed metric), the distribution is positively skewed (right-tailed).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Links mean ≫ median to right-tail outliers pulling the average.

must_hit.point: From E[X]=4 and E[X²]=25: Var = 25−16 = 9 so SD = 3; two zero-variance groups of ten 5s and ten 15s combine to mean 10 and variance 25.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Applies Var = E[X²]−(E[X])² both for the single RV and for the pooled constant groups.

must_hit.point: z = (x−μ)/σ; e.g. x=85, μ=70, σ=5 → z=3.0; binomial P(X=3) for n=5, p=0.6 is 0.3456; Poisson P(X=0) with λ=3 is e^{-3}.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the z formula and at least one of the binomial or Poisson evaluations correctly.

probes: Scores have mean 60 and SD 8; after multiplying by 1.2 and adding 5, what are the new mean and SD?
Given E[X]=4 and E[X²]=25, what is SD(X)? What is the variance of ten 5s combined with ten 15s?

hints.1: For means, think totals (n×mean) and weighted sums; for spread, remember only the multiplier scales SD.
hints.2: Use Var = E[X²]−(E[X])²; for affine transforms only |a| hits SD; for skew compare mean to median.

phases.goal: Contrast absolute correlation strength vs sign, correlation vs causation, LLN vs CLT roles, and the frequentist meaning of a confidence interval versus naive probability talk.

must_hit.point: Linear-relationship strength is |ρ|; e.g. −0.85 is stronger than 0.75 because the negative sign only marks an inverse direction.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Picks −0.85 over 0.75 by comparing absolute values.

must_hit.point: Correlation does not imply causation: strong ice-cream/shark-attack correlation is best explained by a confounding variable such as summer weather.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Rejects causal stories and names a shared lurking cause.

must_hit.point: Law of Large Numbers: as n grows, the sample mean converges to the true expected value (location); Central Limit Theorem describes the shape of the sampling distribution of the mean.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates LLN (mean → expectation) from CLT (sampling-distribution shape).

must_hit.point: A 95% confidence interval like [1.2 s, 2.8 s] means that in repeated sampling, 95% of such intervals would contain the true mean—not that the fixed mean has a 95% probability of lying in this one interval.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the long-run coverage of the procedure and rejects the single-interval probability claim.

probes: Which correlation is stronger, 0.75 or −0.85, and does ice-cream/shark correlation prove causation?
A die average moves from 4.5 after 10 rolls toward 3.5 after 10000 rolls—LLN or CLT? How do you interpret a 95% CI?

hints.1: Strength uses magnitude of ρ; causation needs more than association.
hints.2: Compare |ρ|; name a confounder; split LLN (location) vs CLT (shape); CI coverage is about the procedure.
hints.3: |−0.85| > |0.75|; summer weather confounder; LLN explains convergence to 3.5; 95% of repeated CIs cover the true mean.

phases.goal: Apply Bayes base-rate reasoning, empirical-rule tail/band percentages, standard error, and regression-to-the-mean to concrete interview scenarios.

must_hit.point: Rare disease 1%, test 90% sensitive with 10% false positive rate → P(disease | positive) ≈ 8.3% via Bayes; base-rate neglect wrongly treats this as ~90%.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Sets up P(D|+)=0.009/0.108 ≈ 8.3% and explains false positives from the 99% healthy swamp true positives.

must_hit.point: Spam prior 20%, P(viagra|spam)=50%, P(viagra|not spam)=1% → P(spam|viagra) ≈ 92.6%.
Heights N(170 cm, 10 cm): share between 160 cm and 190 cm is about 81.5% (34% left of μ plus 47.5% up to +2σ); data strictly above z=2 is 2.5%.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Combines half of 68% with half of 95%, and splits the 5% outside ±2σ into two 2.5% tails.

must_hit.point: SE of the sample mean is σ/√n; with μ=100, σ=20, n=25 → SE=4. Extreme first-review scores improving later without intervention is regression to the mean.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives SE=20/5=4 and names regression to the mean for extreme-then-closer retests.

probes: Disease prevalence 1%, sensitivity 90%, false positive rate 10%: given a positive test, what is P(disease)?
What percent of a normal lies above z=2, and what is SE for σ=20 with n=25?

hints.1: Write Bayes with prior × likelihood over total positive probability; use the empirical rule for tails.
hints.2: P(+)=0.90×0.01 + 0.10×0.99; above z=2 is half of the 5% outside ±2σ; SE=σ/√n.

tradeoffs.topic: Absolute correlation strength vs sign of ρ
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Strength of linear association is |ρ|; −0.85 beats 0.75 because the sign only indicates inverse direction, not weakness.
A strong positive link (e.g. ice cream sales and shark attacks) does not imply one causes the other; a confounder such as summer weather can drive both.

tradeoffs.topic: Law of Large Numbers vs Central Limit Theorem
tradeoffs.strong_answer: LLN says the sample mean converges to the true expectation as n grows (location); CLT describes the shape of the sampling distribution of the mean.
Mean is pulled by outliers; median is robust. Mean much larger than median (e.g. 45 vs 15) signals a positively skewed, right-tailed distribution.
Variance is in squared units; SD is in the original units and is what we usually interpret—always take √variance to get SD.

gotchas.trap: Reporting variance when asked for standard deviation (or treating them as interchangeable).
gotchas.correction: Variance is squared units; SD = √variance is in original units—e.g. from Var=9 you must report SD=3.

gotchas.trap: Base-rate neglect: treating a 90% sensitive test as implying ~90% disease probability after a positive result.
gotchas.correction: With 1% prevalence and 10% false positives, Bayes yields ≈8.3%; false positives from the 99% healthy dominate true positives.

gotchas.trap: Reading a 95% CI as '95% probability the true mean lies in this interval' or as covering 95% of individual observations.
gotchas.correction: The parameter is fixed; 95% is the long-run fraction of intervals from the same procedure that contain the true mean.

gotchas.trap: Choosing the correlation with larger algebraic value (e.g. 0.75) over a more negative one (e.g. −0.85) as 'stronger'.
gotchas.correction: Compare |ρ|; −0.85 is the strongest linear association among the usual MCQ options.
